```{python setup}
def hatch_wall(ax, x, y0, y1, side=1, n=7, size=0.28, color=INK, lw=1.3):
    """A fixed-support wall: a solid line with hatching on one side."""
    ax.plot([x, x], [y0, y1], color=color, lw=lw * 1.4, zorder=6)
    for yv in np.linspace(y0, y1, n):
        ax.plot([x, x + side * size], [yv, yv - size], color=color, lw=lw,
                zorder=6)
```

# Strong form of the boundary value problem (Poisson)

::: {.derivation}
Given $f : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$, $g : \Gamma_g \to \mathbb{R}$, and
$h : \Gamma_h \to \mathbb{R}$, find $u : \bar\Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ such that

$$
-\nabla\cdot\left(\underline{\underline{K}}\nabla u\right)
= -\left(K_{ij}u_{,j}\right)_{,i} = f
\qquad \text{in } \Omega
$$

$$
u = g \qquad \text{on } \Gamma_g
$$

$$
\left(\underline{\underline{K}}\nabla u\right)\cdot\underline{n}
= K_{ij}u_{,j}\,n_i = h
\qquad \text{on } \Gamma_h
$$
:::

```{python fig_domain}
#| echo: false
#| output: false

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.0, 5.2))

X, Y = r * np.cos(t), r * np.sin(t)

topmask = (t > 0.30 * math.pi) & (t < 0.62 * math.pi)
botmask = (t > 1.18 * math.pi) & (t < 1.55 * math.pi)

ax.plot(X[topmask], Y[topmask], color=FLUXCLR, lw=3.4, zorder=4)
ax.plot(X[botmask], Y[botmask], color=FLUXCLR, lw=3.4, zorder=4)

ax.text(0.0, 0.0, r"$\Omega$", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=18, color=INK)
```

# In one dimension

::: {.derivation}
$$
-\left(K u_{,x}\right)_{,x} = f \qquad \text{in } \Omega
\qquad\qquad
u = g \qquad \text{on } \Gamma_g
\qquad\qquad
(Ku_{,x})\,n = h \qquad \text{on } \Gamma_h
$$
:::

The one-dimensional boundary $\Gamma$ is just the two endpoints, so $n$ can only be $-1$
or $+1$ — the outward normal at the left end always points in $-x$, and at the right end
always in $+x$.

```{python fig_examples}
#| echo: false
#| output: false

fig, axes = plt.subplots(4, 1, figsize=(8.4, 6.4))

def bar(ax, left_kind, right_kind, n_left_label=None, n_right_label=None):
    # "fixed" = Dirichlet (u=g, drawn as a hatched wall); "free" = Neumann
    # (flux h prescribed, drawn as simply an open end -- there is no support)
    L = 6.0
    ax.plot([0, L], [0, 0], color=INK, lw=2.6, zorder=3)
    if left_kind == "fixed":
        hatch_wall(ax, 0.0, -0.5, 0.5, side=-1, n=6, size=0.34)
    if right_kind == "fixed":
        hatch_wall(ax, L, -0.5, 0.5, side=1, n=6, size=0.34)
    ax.text(-0.05, 0.85, "$x=0$", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=11,
            color=INK)
    ax.text(L + 0.05, 0.85, "$x=L$", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=11,
            color=INK)
    if n_left_label:
        ax.annotate("", xy=(-1.15, 0.0), xytext=(-0.05, 0.0),
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=REACTCLR, lw=1.5,
                                    mutation_scale=11), zorder=5)
        ax.text(-1.3, 0.0, n_left_label, ha="right", va="center",
                fontsize=11.5, color=REACTCLR)
    if n_right_label:
        ax.annotate("", xy=(L + 1.15, 0.0), xytext=(L + 0.05, 0.0),
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=REACTCLR, lw=1.5,
                                    mutation_scale=11), zorder=5)
        ax.text(L + 1.3, 0.0, n_right_label, ha="left", va="center",
                fontsize=11.5, color=REACTCLR)
    tidy(ax)
    ax.set_xlim(-2.4, L + 2.4)
    ax.set_ylim(-1.1, 1.5)

bar(axes[0], "fixed", "fixed")
bar(axes[1], "free", "fixed", n_left_label="$n=-1$")
bar(axes[2], "fixed", "free", n_right_label="$n=+1$")
bar(axes[3], "free", "free", n_left_label="$n=-1$", n_right_label="$n=+1$")

fig.subplots_adjust(hspace=0.75)
fig_examples_path = save(fig, "C4_Fig2_Examples.png")
```

::: {.step}
The Neumann boundary is wherever a flux $h$ is prescribed instead of a value $g$. At the
left end, the outward normal is $-1$; at the right end, it is $+1$ — that sign is why the
Neumann condition in one dimension is written $-u_{,x}(0) = h$ but $+u_{,x}(L) = h$: both
are $(Ku_{,x})\cdot n = h$ once $K=1$ is included and $n$ is substituted in.
:::

# Coming from the exact solution

Last time, we found the exact solution to the 1D Poisson problem to be

::: {.derivation}
$$
u(x) = g + (1-x)h + \int_x^1\left(\int_0^y f(z)\,dz\right)dy
$$
:::

::: {.step}
So we're done... why do anything more?
:::

::: {.step .notes}
- What if we don't have a simple function $f$?
- What if the domain is not one-dimensional?
:::

Want to convert this into a representation we can compute on. **Idea:** use an inner
product and function space to "describe" our function.

::: {.derivation}
$$
\mathcal{S} = \left\{\, u \in H^1(\Omega) \;\middle|\; u(x) = g(x) \text{ for } x \in \Gamma_g \,\right\}
\qquad \leftarrow \textbf{trial function space}
$$

$$
\mathcal{V} = \left\{\, w \in H^1(\Omega) \;\middle|\; w(x) = 0 \text{ for } x \in \Gamma_g \,\right\}
\qquad \leftarrow \textbf{test function space}
$$
:::

::: {.step}
Recall $H^1(\Omega) = \left\{ f : \Omega \to \mathbb{R} \;\middle|\;
\int_\Omega f^2 + \nabla f \cdot \nabla f \; d\Omega < \infty \right\}$ — in 1D, these are
continuous functions. (See the [function-space appendix](3_Support_FunctionSpaces.qmd) for
more.)
:::

# Weak form of the boundary value problem

::: {.derivation}
Given $f : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$, $g : \Gamma_g \to \mathbb{R}$, $h : \Gamma_h \to \mathbb{R}$,
and $\underline{\underline{K}} : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}^{n_{sd} \times n_{sd}}$ symmetric
positive definite, find $u \in \mathcal{S}$ such that for every $w \in \mathcal{V}$,

$$
(\mathrm{W}) \qquad
\int_\Omega \nabla w \cdot \underline{\underline{K}} \nabla u \; d\Omega
= \int_\Omega wf\;d\Omega + \int_{\Gamma_h} wh\;d\Gamma
$$
:::

In one dimension, this is

::: {.derivation}
$$
(\mathrm{W}) \qquad
\int_0^L w_{,x}\,K\,u_{,x}\;dx
= \int_0^L wf\;dx + w u_{,x}\Big\rvert_{x=0}^{x=L}
\qquad \text{or, in our case,} \qquad
\int_0^L w_{,x}\,K\,u_{,x}\;dx = \int_0^1 wf\;dx + w(0)\,h
$$
:::

# What does this mean?

::: {.step}
**Example:** put an object in a bag, try to guess the object.
:::

::: {.step .notes}
- → bag size is the "space" of objects you're guessing in
- → people can come look in the bag & describe with 1 word
:::

::: {.step}
(In class, a mousetrap toy.)
:::

The words are what we use to "test" or "measure" our object against.

If we have all possible descriptors, we should know precisely what the object is.
Otherwise, we pick a set of "best" words with which to describe.

::: {.step}
Think about this — it is sort of the way we come to know God.
:::

::: {.step .notes}
- → descriptors, experiences, etc., but we have limited knowledge; at some point we will
  know — John 17:3
:::

# Formal proof of equivalence (strong $\Rightarrow$ weak)

Start from the strong form and multiply by an arbitrary $w$, then integrate over $\Omega$:

::: {.derivation}
$$
-\nabla\cdot\left(\underline{\underline{K}}\nabla u\right) = f
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
-\int_\Omega w\,\nabla\cdot\left(\underline{\underline{K}}\nabla u\right)\,d\Omega
= \int_\Omega wf\,d\Omega
\qquad (w \text{ arbitrary})
$$
:::

The left side needs the **product rule**, applied to $\nabla\cdot(w\underline{\underline{K}}\nabla u)$:

::: {.derivation}
$$
\nabla\cdot\left(w\,\underline{\underline{K}}\nabla u\right)
= \nabla w\cdot\underline{\underline{K}}\nabla u
+ w\,\nabla\cdot\left(\underline{\underline{K}}\nabla u\right)
$$
:::

so that, integrating the left side and applying the **Divergence Theorem**,

::: {.derivation}
$$
\int_\Omega \nabla\cdot\left(w\,\underline{\underline{K}}\nabla u\right) d\Omega
= \int_\Gamma \left(w\,\underline{\underline{K}}\nabla u\right)\cdot \underline{n}\;d\Gamma
$$
:::

Combining these two facts, the term we wanted rearranges into

::: {.derivation}
$$
-\left(\int_\Gamma \left(w\,\underline{\underline{K}}\nabla u\right)\cdot\underline{n}\;d\Gamma
- \int_\Omega \nabla w \cdot \underline{\underline{K}}\nabla u \;d\Omega\right)
= \int_\Omega wf\,d\Omega
$$
:::

::: {.derivation}
$$
\Longrightarrow \qquad
\int_\Omega \nabla w \cdot \underline{\underline{K}}\nabla u \; d\Omega
= \int_\Omega wf\,d\Omega + \int_\Gamma \left(w\,\underline{\underline{K}}\nabla u\right)\cdot\underline{n}\;d\Gamma
$$
:::

::: {.derivation}
$$
\Longrightarrow \qquad
\int_\Omega w_{,i}K_{ij}u_{,j}\;d\Omega
= \int_\Omega wf\,d\Omega + \int_\Gamma w K_{ij}u_{,j}\,n_i\;d\Gamma
$$
:::

::: {.step}
But $w(x) = 0$ on $\Gamma_g$, and $\Gamma = \Gamma_g \cup \Gamma_h$, so the boundary
integral only survives over $\Gamma_h$ — where the strong form tells us
$K_{ij}u_{,j}n_i = h$:
:::

::: {.derivation}
$$
\boxed{\int_\Omega w_{,i}K_{ij}u_{,j}\;d\Omega
= \int_\Omega wf\,d\Omega + \int_{\Gamma_h} wh\;d\Gamma}
$$
:::

which is exactly $(\mathrm{W})$. The next class continues the other direction —
$(\mathrm{W}) \Rightarrow (\mathrm{S})$ — which is a genuinely different (and more
delicate) argument.
